TS1450, Dynamic imports can only accept a module specifier and an optional set of attributes as arguments, import() no arguments, diagnostic category message

This is the behavior in every version I tried: 5.9.3, 6.0.3, 7.0.2, 7.1.0-dev.20261103.1 (typescript@next) and main e2bc2bcb. Not a regression.

```
export {};
import();
import("./t.js", {}, "");
import(...["./t.js"]);
```

`tsc --noEmit --target esnext --module esnext --pretty false t.ts`:
```
t.ts(2,1): message TS1450: Dynamic imports can only accept a module specifier and an optional set of attributes as arguments
t.ts(3,1): message TS1450: Dynamic imports can only accept a module specifier and an optional set of attributes as arguments
t.ts(4,8): error TS1325: Argument of dynamic import cannot be spread element.
```
TS1450 is printed as `message`, while the neighbouring grammar error for the same call (TS1325) is an `error`. The language server maps category Message to `DiagnosticSeverity.Information` (`diagnosticSeverity` in `internal/ls/lsconv/converters.go`), so in the editor `import()` gets an information marker instead of an error, and tools that filter diagnostics by category treat the file as error-free.

`error TS1450: …`, like the other grammar errors on import calls. Both calls are syntax errors: `ImportCall : import ( AssignmentExpression ,opt ) | import ( AssignmentExpression , AssignmentExpression ,opt )` (https://tc39.es/ecma262/#sec-import-calls). node rejects the file with `SyntaxError: import() requires a specifier`.

In `internal/diagnostics/diagnosticMessages.json` the entry has `"category": "Message", "code": 1450`. Among codes below 3000 it is the only Message-category entry that reports a problem in the user's code; the other Message entries are "File is included via …" explanations, quick-fix titles and option descriptions (it sits right after 1449, an option description). Changing the category to "Error" and regenerating would turn `message TS1450` into `error TS1450` in the 8 reference baselines that contain it (`importAssertion1`, `importAttributes1`, `importCallExpressionGrammarError`, `importSource5`, `importSource11`, `plainJSGrammarErrors`).

Native tsc: GetEmitModuleFormatOfFile ignores content-mapper VirtualFileName (*.mts treated as CJS under module:commonjs)

content mapper, VirtualFileName, GetEmitModuleFormatOfFile, GetImpliedNodeFormatForEmit, ImpliedNodeFormat, .mts, module commonjs

- Present on current `main` (native Go port)
- During load, `filesparser` correctly sets `SourceFileMetaData.ImpliedNodeFormat` from `VirtualFileName` (e.g. `app.box.mts` → ESNext)
- But `Program.GetEmitModuleFormatOfFile` / `GetImpliedNodeFormatForEmit` pass the physical `FileName()` (e.g. `app.box`) into `GetImpliedNodeFormatForEmitWorker`

N/A (content mapper / program API)

Content mapper that sets output extension `.mts` for `app.box`, with:

```
{ "compilerOptions": { "module": "commonjs", "moduleResolution": "node10" }, "contentMappers": [{ "package": "mapper", "extensions": [".box"] }] }
```

```
// app.box  (mapped virtual name: app.box.mts)
export const value = 1;
```

Observed via program API after opening a project that loads the mapped file:

```
mapped.VirtualFileName()                          == "/home/project/app.box.mts"
meta.ImpliedNodeFormat                            == ESNext
GetEmitModuleFormatOfFileWorker(VirtualFileName)  == ESNext
GetEmitModuleFormatOfFileWorker(FileName)         == CommonJS   // fallback to options
program.GetEmitModuleFormatOfFile(mapped)         == CommonJS   // uses FileName
program.GetImpliedNodeFormatForEmit(mapped)       == None       // uses FileName
```

Root cause in `tsc/internal/compiler/program.go`:

```
func (p *Program) GetEmitModuleFormatOfFile(sourceFile ast.HasFileName) core.ModuleKind {
	return ast.GetEmitModuleFormatOfFileWorker(sourceFile.FileName(), ...)
}
func (p *Program) GetImpliedNodeFormatForEmit(sourceFile ast.HasFileName) core.ResolutionMode {
	return ast.GetImpliedNodeFormatForEmitWorker(sourceFile.FileName(), ...)
}
```

For non-`node16`/`nodenext` emit module kinds, `GetImpliedNodeFormatForEmitWorker` only keeps `ImpliedNodeFormat == ESNext` when `package.json#type` is `"module"` **or** the **filename** ends in `.mjs`/`.mts`. The physical `.box` name fails that gate, so format falls back to `compilerOptions.module` (CommonJS). The same pattern affects `GetModeForUsageLocation` / `GetEmitSyntaxForUsageLocation`.

Note: under `module: nodenext` the worker returns `metadata.ImpliedNodeFormat` directly, so the bug is masked there.

An ESM-mapped content-mapper file (`VirtualFileName` `*.mts`, `ImpliedNodeFormat` ESNext) reports emit/implied format as CommonJS / None under `module: commonjs`, so downstream emit/module transformers and format diagnostics see CJS.

When `VirtualFileName` is set, emit/implied format (and usage-location mode helpers) should use it — consistent with load-time metadata derivation in `filesparser.go` — so `*.mts` mapped outputs stay ESM under `module: commonjs`.

Same helpers also take `FileName()` in:

- `GetModeForUsageLocation`
- `GetEmitSyntaxForUsageLocation`

Root cause in `tsc/internal/scanner/scanner.go` (`isConflictMarkerTrivia`, ~2422–2425):

atLineStart := pos == 0 || stringutil.IsLineBreak(rune(text[pos-1]))

Hello! TypeScript is my favorite language. Thank you all for working so hard on it!
I have some ideas that could make TypeScript even better and more powerful. All of these suggestions are related to the type system.

---

Currently, accessing the `length` property of a string literal type yields only `number`. I suggest returning the actual length value.
For example, `'test'['length']` currently gives `number`, but it would be amazing if it evaluated to `4`.

> **Reason:** Tuple types already support this behavior: `[1, 2, 3]['length']` gives `3`, not an abstract `number`. It would be consistent to bring this feature to string literal types as well.

If there are concerns about IntelliSense performance, we could look at how it was successfully optimized for tuples.

---

Similarly, accessing a tuple element by index works perfectly: `[1, 2, 3][1]` gives `2`.
However, for string literals, `'123'[1]` gives the generic `string` type instead of `'2'`.

> **Reason:** In JavaScript runtime, `'123'[1]` evaluates to `'2'`. Having the type system mirror this would prevent type loss when dealing with string manipulation.

Since this is a direct index lookup, it shouldn't negatively impact IntelliSense performance.

---

Yes, it is currently possible to implement an `IndexOf<A, V>` utility using recursion, but supporting multiple spreads would make the code significantly more human-readable.

For example, I would love to be able to write:
```
type IndexOf<A extends any[], V> =
    A extends [...infer I extends any[], V, ...any[]] ? I['length'] : -1;

type Test = IndexOf<[1, 2, 3], 2>; // Currently gives: number (or drops into unknown/error) -> Expected: 1
type Test_2 = IndexOf<[1, 2, 3, 2, 1], 2>; // Expected: 1 | 3 (union of all matching indices)
```

**Proposed implementation strategy to protect IntelliSense speed:**
* If there is **one or no** spread elements in the `extends` clause, use the current fast-path algorithm.
* If there are **two or more** spread elements, switch to a multi-splitting evaluation (evaluating all possible permutation variants), just like in the example above.

---

When I first started learning TypeScript, I thought it was just a small "linter-like" add-on, not a fully-fledged language. But once I discovered **mapped types**, smart **conditional extends**, and the algebraic nature of **never**, **unknown**, and **any**, I realized that TypeScript is an incredibly powerful, useful, and comfortable language.

Thank you for your amazing work, and I hope you will consider these ideas for future versions of TypeScript!

A mapper with `dynamicConfig: true` returns the files its configuration depends on in `openProject`'s `watchedFiles`. If one of those files is a `.ts` file that the user edits in the editor, the mapper's types never update after the file is saved.

  "contentMappers": [{ "package": "toy-mapper", "extensions": [".kinds"] }],
  "include": ["*.ts"]
}
```

`kinds.ts` (the mapper's configuration; the mapper reads it from disk)

```
export default ["A", "B"];
```

`values.kinds` (any non-empty text; the mapper ignores it)

```
# the content of this file is ignored; the toy mapper reads kinds.ts
```

`index.ts`

```
import values from "./values.kinds";

// Error while kinds.ts lists "A" and "B". The error goes away once kinds.ts lists only "A".
export const first: "A" = values[0];
```

`toy-mapper/package.json`

```
{
  "name": "toy-mapper",
  "version": "1.0.0",
  "type": "module",
  "typescript": {
    "contentMapper": { "exec": ["node", "server.js"], "compilerOptions": [], "dynamicConfig": true }
  }
}
```

`toy-mapper/server.js`

```
import { createHash } from "node:crypto";
import { readFileSync } from "node:fs";
import path from "node:path";

const projects = new Map();

function readKinds(configFileName) {
  const file = path.join(path.dirname(configFileName), "kinds.ts");
  const list = JSON.parse(/\[.*\]/.exec(readFileSync(file, "utf8"))[0]);
  return { file, list };
[... 41 more lines]
```

`npx tsc --noEmit --runExternalCode` reports `Type '"A" | "B"' is not assignable to type '"A"'` for `index.ts`, and reports nothing after `kinds.ts` is changed to `["A"]`, as expected.

Steps, at the protocol level (`tsc --lsp --stdio` with `initializationOptions: { runExternalCode: true }`):

1. `didOpen` `index.ts` and `kinds.ts`. `index.ts` has the error.
2. `didChange` `kinds.ts` to `export default ["A"];` and pull diagnostics once, as an editor does after an edit.
3. Write `kinds.ts` to disk, then send `didSave` and `workspace/didChangeWatchedFiles` for it.
4. The error in `index.ts` stays. Restarting the language server removes it.

The error in `index.ts` stays after `kinds.ts` is saved. Driven through `tsc --lsp --stdio` the way an editor does (an editor asks for diagnostics after every edit). Between the edit and the save the client pulls diagnostics once; this matters, see "Additional information about the issue".

Trace of what reaches the mapper (client events and mapper calls on one clock):

```
CLIENT textDocument/didChange kinds.ts        <- user types in kinds.ts, buffer now lists only "A"
mapper <- closeProject
mapper <- openProject  config=tsconfig.json   <- re-read, but kinds.ts on disk still says ["A","B"]
mapper -> openProject  identity=b64e3448
CLIENT (client pulls diagnostics)
CLIENT disk write kinds.ts                    <- user saves
CLIENT textDocument/didSave kinds.ts
CLIENT workspace/didChangeWatchedFiles kinds.ts
                                               <- no mapper call at all; types stay stale
```

Time until the error in `index.ts` goes away (3 s timeout):

| What happens to `kinds.ts` | Result |
|---|---|
| Not open in the editor: written on disk, `didChangeWatchedFiles` sent | updated after 9 ms |
| Open: edit, pull diagnostics, then save (`didChange`, disk write, `didSave`, `didChangeWatchedFiles`) | still stale after 3 s |
| ...then close the tab | still stale after 3 s |
| ...then close and reopen it | still stale after 3 s |
| ...then edit `index.ts` | still stale after 3 s |
| ...then type one more character in `kinds.ts` (`didChange`) | updated after 5 ms |

As documented in https://github.com/microsoft/typescript-go/pull/4712 ("TypeScript watches the absolute paths returned in `watchedFiles`. A change invalidates only projects that reported that path, closes their current mapper project configuration, obtains a fresh identity and watch set, and performs a normal project rebuild"), saving a file listed in `watchedFiles` should re-run `openProject`, whether or not the file is open in the editor.

Related to #64943 (a change on disk to a content-mapped file does not refresh diagnostics), but the cause is different, and #64944 does not touch this code path.

`tsc/internal/project/overlayfs.go` (main, lines 534-538), in `processChanges`:

```
if events.watchChanged && o == nil {
    result.Changed.Add(uri)
}

if len(events.changes) > 0 && o != nil {
    result.Changed.Add(uri)
    ...
```

A watch event adds the file to `result.Changed` only when it is not open (`o == nil`). When it is open, the overlay is the source of truth, which is right for files TypeScript reads itself. A content mapper reads `watchedFiles` from disk, so an open file is the case where the overlay and the disk differ.

`refreshContentMapperProjectForChanges` (`projectcollectionbuilder.go`, main, line 474, called from `DidChangeFiles` at line 413) only looks at the paths in `summary.Changed`/`Deleted`/`Created`. So for an open watched file, the only thing that re-runs `openProject` is `didChange`, and at that moment the file on disk still has the old content. The save that follows reaches `processChanges` as a `Save` and a `WatchChange` for a file with an overlay, and neither adds it to `Changed`.

If the client sends no request between the edit and the save, the pending `didChange`, `didSave` and watch event are flushed together, `Changed` contains the file, and `openProject` reads the saved file. So the problem shows up only in an editor, which sends requests continuously.

A possible fix: also record watch changes of files that have an overlay (for example in a separate set on the summary) and let `refreshContentMapperProjectForChanges` consider them, or treat a save of a file in `contentMapperWatchedFiles` as an invalidation.

API: `tsc.exe` opens a visible console window on Windows when the parent process has no console

windowsHide, tsc.exe console window, API console window Windows spawn, SyncRpcChannel, ELECTRON_RUN_AS_NODE, cmd window opens, console window flash Windows, conhost tsc

- This is the behavior in every version I tried, and I reviewed the FAQ for entries about Windows console windows and the API

I reproduced this on 7.0.2, 7.1.0-beta, and 7.1.0-dev.20261031.1. TypeScript 6.0.3 does not export this API.

Install `typescript@next` in an empty directory on Windows and add these two files.

`api-console.mjs` (on 7.0.2, import from `typescript/unstable/sync`):

```
import { API } from "typescript/sync";

const api = new API({ cwd: process.cwd() });
setTimeout(() => api.close(), 8_000);
```

`launch.mjs` (replace the path with your VS Code installation):

```
import { spawn } from "node:child_process";

const env = { ...process.env, ELECTRON_RUN_AS_NODE: "1" };
spawn("C:/path/to/Microsoft VS Code/Code.exe", ["api-console.mjs"], {
  detached: true,
  stdio: "ignore",
  env,
}).unref();
```

Run `node launch.mjs`.

`detached: true` starts `Code.exe` without a console. Running `api-console.mjs` directly with Node from a terminal does not show the problem.

A console window opens and stays open until the API closes. Its title is the path of `tsc.exe`. In my environment, Windows Terminal is the default terminal application, so the window opens in Windows Terminal.

This is wrong because the API communicates through pipes, so users have no reason to see this window. Tools that start one API for each project or restart the API open several windows. I found this in a VS Code extension.

`tsc.exe` runs without a visible window, regardless of whether the parent process has a console.

`Code.exe` is a GUI subsystem program, so it has no console even when it runs with `ELECTRON_RUN_AS_NODE=1`. Windows therefore creates a new console for `tsc.exe`. Other Electron-based hosts should behave the same way, but I tested only `Code.exe`.

These calls do not pass `windowsHide` in the published 7.1.0-dev.20261031.1 package:

- `dist/api/syncChannel.js`: the call that starts `tsc.exe` with `--pipe`
- `dist/api/async/client.js`: the call that starts `tsc.exe` with stdio pipes

Passing `windowsHide: true` in these calls should fix the problem. I confirmed this on 7.0.2 with the sync API: the unchanged script opened one window, and a run with `windowsHide: true` added to `spawn` opened none. `tsc.exe` started in both runs. I did not run the async API.

As a workaround, we temporarily replace `child_process.spawn`, call `syncBuiltinESMExports()`, and construct `API`. This works only because the sync API spawns in its constructor, and it depends on internal behavior.

Native tsc reads a literal U+FFFD in a regex character class as 0xEF (false TS1517 / TS1516)

regex U+FFFD, replacement character in regex, character class range, Range out of order in character class, TS1517, TS1516, native tsc, tsgo

- This changed between versions 6.0.3 and 7.0.2. 6.0.3 accepts the code. 7.0.2, 7.1.0-beta and 7.1.0-dev.20261031.1 all report it.

The repro needs a literal U+FFFD character, which tends to get mangled by copy and paste, so this writes the file and runs the nightly:

```
node -e 'require("fs").writeFileSync("repro.ts", "export const r = /[\\uFFF9-\uFFFD]/\n")'
npx -p typescript@next tsc --noEmit repro.ts
```

`repro.ts` ends up as this. The last character in the class is a literal U+FFFD (bytes `EF BF BD`):

```
export const r = /[\uFFF9-�]/
```

```
repro.ts(1,20): error TS1517: Range out of order in character class.
```

U+FFF9 to U+FFFD is in order, so the range is fine. With the `u` flag the same class gets a different wrong error:

```
error TS1516: A character class range must not be bounded by another character class.
```

No error, same as 6.0.3. The regex is valid at runtime and matches U+FFF9 through U+FFFD.

It looks like a literal U+FFFD gets read as 0xEF, the first byte of its UTF-8 encoding. Changing only the start of the range:

| Character class | 6.0.3 | 7.0.2 and 7.1.0-dev.20261031.1 |
|---|---|---|
| `[\u00EF-�]` | ok | ok |
| `[\u00F0-�]` | ok | TS1517 |
| `[\u0100-�]` | ok | TS1517 |
| `[\uFFF9-�]` | ok | TS1517 |
| `[\uFFF9-\uFFFD]` (escaped) | ok | ok |

A lone literal U+FFFD (`/�/`) and one that starts a range (`/[�-\uFFFF]/`) are both fine on all three versions, and so is a string literal: `const s: "\uFFFD" = "�"` type-checks. So it seems specific to the regex scanner.

My guess, without having read the code: Go's `utf8.RuneError` is U+FFFD, so a check like `r == utf8.RuneError` treats a real U+FFFD as invalid UTF-8 unless it also looks at the size (3 bytes for a real U+FFFD, 1 for bad input).

I ran into this in a test that checks some text has no characters in that block, and worked around it with the escaped form.

7.0 regression: inherited members are sorted by position, so an empty subinterface changes assignability

inherited members order, member order, property order, interface extends, empty subinterface, variance, unmeasurable, getNamedMembers, createMemberLayout, missing TS2322, 7.0 regression

- This changed between versions 6.0.3 and 7.0.2
- Still present in 7.1.0-dev.20261030.1.
- microsoft/typescript-go#1987 (first in `@typescript/native-preview` 7.0.0-dev.20251031.1) fixed this for one level of inheritance (`B` below), but not for two (`C`).

(Reproduction repo can be found [here](https://github.com/pearofducks/ts7-reproduction) - it doesn't seem like Playground runs an applicable version for this issue).

```
export const empty: C<string> = {};
declare const narrowB: B<{ a: string }>;
export const wideB: B<{ a: string; b?: number }> = narrowB;
declare const narrowC: C<{ a: string }>;
export const wideC: C<{ a: string; b?: number }> = narrowC;

interface A<T> {
  inherited: () => T;
}
interface B<T> extends A<T> {
[... 3 more lines]
```

Run with `tsc --noEmit --pretty false deep.ts` and no tsconfig, since `strict` is the default. `empty` is only there for its message, which lists `C`'s members in the order the checker compares them.

With 7.0.2 and 7.1.0-dev.20261030.1, `wideC` compiles, though `C` adds nothing to `B` and the same assignment to `B` is an error:

```
deep.ts(1,14): error TS2739: Type '{}' is missing the following properties from type 'C<string>': inherited, own
deep.ts(3,14): error TS2322: Type 'B<{ a: string; }>' is not assignable to type 'B<{ a: string; b?: number | undefined; }>'.
  The types returned by 'own(...)' are incompatible between these types.
    Property 'b' is missing in type 'Required<{ a: string; }>' but required in type 'Required<{ a: string; b?: number | undefined; }>'.
```

`wideC` is an error, like `wideB`, as in 6.0.3:

```
deep.ts(1,14): error TS2739: Type '{}' is missing the following properties from type 'C<string>': own, inherited
deep.ts(3,14): error TS2322: Type 'B<{ a: string; }>' is not assignable to type 'B<{ a: string; b?: number | undefined; }>'.
  The types returned by 'own(...)' are incompatible between these types.
    Property 'b' is missing in type 'Required<{ a: string; }>' but required in type 'Required<{ a: string; b?: number | undefined; }>'.
deep.ts(5,14): error TS2322: Type 'C<{ a: string; }>' is not assignable to type 'C<{ a: string; b?: number | undefined; }>'.
  The types returned by 'own(...)' are incompatible between these types.
    Property 'b' is missing in type 'Required<{ a: string; }>' but required in type 'Required<{ a: string; b?: number | undefined; }>'.
```

`C` has no members of its own, so all of its properties are inherited, and they are sorted by declaration position (`getNamedMembers` in 7.0.2, `createMemberLayout` on `main`): `inherited`, declared in `A`, comes before `own`, declared in `B`. 6.0 takes `C`'s inherited members from `B` in `B`'s order, which puts `B`'s own members first: `own, inherited`.

The order changes assignability through variance measurement, which relates `C` to `C<Super>` and back member by member, stopping at the first member that fails. `Required<T>` in `own` marks `T` unmeasurable (the `-?`), but only when relating `C<Super>` to `C`, and that direction fails at `inherited` first when `inherited` comes first. `T` is then measured plain invariant: `--generateTrace` shows `B` as `[in out (unmeasurable)]` and `C` as `[in out]`. Invariant, `wideC` passes because `{ a: string }` and `{ a: string; b?: number }` are each assignable to the other, while `wideB` gets the structural check that finds `own`'s return types incompatible.

A fix: order inherited members by base type, and within a base type in that base's order, as 6.0 does.

Related, and already fixed on `main`: in 7.0.2 the order could also depend on other files. An inherited member counted as the interface's own when its text range fell inside the range of one of the interface's declarations in another file, such as a module augmentation, because `isDeclarationContainedBy` doesn't compare files, so a longer comment in an augmentation could make an assignment compile. #64915 replaced that check for classes and interfaces (first in 7.1.0-dev.20261024.1). I can share a repro if it matters for 7.0.

Found because a library relies on a `-?` member like `own` for exact assignments between instantiations of its schema type, and interfaces extending that type lost them on 7.0.

#64096 added this overload in `lib.es2026.json.d.ts`:

```

`reviver` is required here, but it is optional in `lib.es5.d.ts` and in the spec (`JSON.parse ( text [ , reviver ] )`):

parse(text: string, reviver?: (this: any, key: string, value: any) => any): any;

- `.call` and `.apply` under `strictBindCallApply`

parse(text: string, reviver?: (this: any, key: string, value: any, context: { source?: string }) => any): any;
```

```

Steps:

```
4. Send workspace/didChangeWatchedFiles (type Created) for new.ts, then textDocument/didOpen it. The other order gives the same result.

new.ts is served by the parent project (lib: ES2015) instead of apps/web/tsconfig.json, so it gets false errors:

(plus a follow-on TS7006 for the lambda parameter losing its contextual type)

Cause (at commit 4163ca172f): for a file Created event, configfileregistrybuilder.go (~line 613) only checks ParsedCommandLine.PossiblyMatchesFileName, which matches against globs from WildcardDirectoryGlobs() (tsoptions/parsedcommandline.go ~317–318 and ~511–513). Those globs are built as <wildcardDir>/**/*.{ts,...} straight from the raw directory path, so:
- "[ws]" doesn't parse as a glob; the parse error is ignored and the glob is silently dropped.
- "{ws}" / "{b,c}" are read as alternation groups and "app[1-2]" as a character range, so the real folder name never matches.
- Matching is exact-case, even on case-insensitive filesystems.

Either escape the special characters, or check the new file directly against the wildcard directories using caseSensitivity.PathKey (recursive dirs contain it, non-recursive dirs equal its parent, extension is supported). - This changed between versions 6.0.3 and 7.0.2.
- It reproduces with `7.0.2`, `7.1.0-beta` and `7.1.0-dev.20261026.1`.

Not applicable, since the bug is in the scanner exported from `typescript/ast`.

```
import { createScanner, SyntaxKind } from "typescript/ast";

const scanner = createScanner(false, 0, "a # b");
for (let i = 0; i < 6; i++) {
    const kind = scanner.scan();
    console.log(kind === SyntaxKind.PrivateIdentifier ? "PrivateIdentifier" : kind, scanner.getTokenStart(), scanner.getTokenEnd());
    if (kind === SyntaxKind.EndOfFile) break;
}
```

The scanner never gets past a `#` that is not followed by an identifier character. Every `scan()` from there on returns a zero-width `PrivateIdentifier` at the same offset, so a loop that scans until `EndOfFile` never terminates.

```
79 0 1
5 1 2
PrivateIdentifier 2 2
PrivateIdentifier 2 2
PrivateIdentifier 2 2
PrivateIdentifier 2 2
```

As in 6.0, `ts.createScanner` scans `a # b` as `Identifier 0-1`, `WhitespaceTrivia 1-2`, `PrivateIdentifier 2-3` (reporting "Invalid character"), `WhitespaceTrivia 3-4`, `Identifier 4-5` and `EndOfFileToken 5-5`.

The lone-`#` branch of the API scanner sets `tokenValue = "#"` without advancing `pos`:

https://github.com/microsoft/TypeScript/blob/8a62bbe746909624b69b6e671026b454da2f02cf/packages/typescript/src/ast/scanner.ts#L1985-L1989

TypeScript 6.0 advances inside its error call there, `error(Diagnostics.Invalid_character, pos++, charSize(ch))`. The Go scanner consumes the `#` in `scanIdentifier(1)` before it reports `Invalid_character`. The port lost both the `pos++` and the diagnostic.

We hit it while scanning a whole JavaScript file for its comment ranges. Without parser context, the body of a regex literal such as `/a#/g` is scanned as tokens, and the scan never finished.

Checking deeply nested array/object literals is quadratic and can hang in TS7

typescript-go, deeply nested, array literal, hang, quadratic, isConstContext

- **7.1.0-dev** (built from main today): slow / hangs
- **7.0.2** (npm): same
- **5.9.3** (JS): failed fast instead (parser `RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded` at ~800 levels)

This is a regression in the Go port in the sense that the JavaScript compiler never hung on these inputs — it bailed out quickly, while TS7 can run for minutes on valid input.

```
// depth-8000 nested array literal — 100% valid TypeScript
const x = [[[[ /* ... */ 1 /* ... */ ]]]];
```

Checking time grows quadratically with the nesting depth and becomes effectively unbounded. Measured with a locally built `built/local/tsc.exe` from main (Windows), `--noEmit --target esnext`:

| Input | main (7.1.0-dev) | TS 5.9.3 (JS) |
|---|---|---|
| array literal, depth 2000 | 0.8s | error (fast parse stack overflow) |
| array literal, depth 4000 | 5.3s | error (fast) |
| array literal, depth 8000 | >30s | error (fast) |
| array literal, depth 100000 | effectively hangs | error (fast) |
| object literal, depth 4000 | 10.8s | error (fast) |

`--extendedDiagnostics` attributes the time to the **check** phase (parse stays flat at ~25ms).

Checking should be linear in the size of the input, and should not take dramatically longer than 5.x on any valid input.

`Checker.isConstContext` recurses up through array/object/parenthesized/property-assignment parents and is invoked once per nesting level, so the total work is O(depth²):

```
func (c *Checker) isConstContext(node *ast.Node) bool {
	parent := node.Parent
	return ast.IsConstAssertion(parent) || ... ||
		(ast.IsParenthesizedExpression(parent) || ast.IsArrayLiteralExpression(parent) || ast.IsSpreadElement(parent)) && c.isConstContext(parent) || ...
}
```

The JavaScript implementation has the same recursion, but its parser throws `RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded` at roughly 800 levels, so the quadratic was never observable there. The Go parser handles much deeper nesting and exposes it.

A fix that caches the per-node result in `NodeLinks` (following the existing `NodeCheckFlagsInitializerIsUndefinedComputed` pattern) makes checking linear: 4000-deep array 5.3s → 0.17s, 8000-deep array >30s → 0.19s, 4000-deep object 10.8s → 0.37s, with unchanged diagnostics. PR to follow.

Stack overflow in getEffectsSignature for long comma-separated call chains (e.g. minified bundles with allowJs)

"Maximum call stack size exceeded", getEffectsSignature, getTypeAtFlowCall, comma expression, assertion, minified bundle, allowJs

- This is a crash
- Reproduces in 4.9.5, 5.9.3 and 6.0.3 (`RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded`).
- On `main` (native compiler) the same recursion happens. It does not crash at these sizes because Go goroutine stacks grow up to 1 GB, but `getEffectsSignature` nests once per call in the chain (about 5,000 deep for the 5,000-call repro below).

The repro is a generated file of about 16 KB, which is too large for a playground link. The script below generates it.

```
node -e '
let s = "declare const a: { f(x: number): void };\nvar first = late;\n";
s += Array.from({ length: 2000 }, () => "a.f(0)").join(", ") + ";\nvar late = a;\n";
require("fs").writeFileSync("repro.ts", s);'
npx -p typescript@6.0.3 tsc --noEmit repro.ts
```

`repro.ts` looks like this:

```
declare const a: { f(x: number): void };
var first = late;
a.f(0), a.f(0), a.f(0), /* ...2000 calls in total... */ a.f(0);
var late = a;
```

The same code with `;` in place of `,` between the calls checks fine.

In practice this shows up when a minified bundle is included in a program with `allowJs` (for example, through the default `include`). Minifiers join statements with commas. One example is the CommonJS build of `lucide-react`, which has thousands of `Object.defineProperty(exports, "...", { get: ... })` calls in a single comma expression.

```
RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded
    at checkNonNullExpression
    at getEffectsSignature
    at getTypeAtFlowCall
    at getTypeAtFlowNode
    at getFlowTypeOfReference
    at checkIdentifier
    at checkExpressionWorker
    at checkExpression
    at checkNonNullExpression
[... 6 more lines]
```

No crash. Only the normal `TS2454: Variable 'late' is used before being assigned.` error is reported, the same as for the statement form.

The binder adds a `FlowCall` node for every call that is an operand of a comma expression, because such a call may be an assertion (`maybeBindExpressionFlowIfCall`, called for both `expr.Left` and `expr.Right` of `,`):
https://github.com/microsoft/TypeScript/blob/8d9b6da99ea7d4a8e7d906dd2532456dfe14e24f/tsc/internal/binder/binder.go#L2165-L2173
https://github.com/microsoft/TypeScript/blob/8d9b6da99ea7d4a8e7d906dd2532456dfe14e24f/tsc/internal/binder/binder.go#L2262-L2270

However, `getEffectsSignature` uses the circularity-safe `getTypeOfDottedName` only when the call's parent is an `ExpressionStatement`. Comma operands fall through to `checkNonNullExpression(node.Expression())`:
https://github.com/microsoft/TypeScript/blob/8d9b6da99ea7d4a8e7d906dd2532456dfe14e24f/tsc/internal/checker/flow.go#L2051-L2067

Checking `a.f` at call *n* runs control flow analysis for `a`, which walks back to the `FlowCall` for call *n-1*. That calls `getEffectsSignature` for call *n-1*, which checks `a.f` there and walks back to call *n-2*, and so on. The recursion is one level per call. It only happens when a reference after the chain is checked before the calls themselves (here `var first = late;` forces `late`'s initializer to be checked first). Otherwise `links.effectsSignature` fills in from left to right.

In the 6.0 JS sources, the code is the same:
https://github.com/microsoft/TypeScript/blob/050880ce59e30b356b686bd3144efe24f875ebc8/src/compiler/checker.ts#L28792-L28817
https://github.com/microsoft/TypeScript/blob/050880ce59e30b356b686bd3144efe24f875ebc8/src/compiler/binder.ts#L1779-L1786

A possible fix is to treat calls whose value is discarded the same way as expression statements: comma operands on the left, and comma operands on the right when the comma expression's own value is unused. Their targets would be resolved with `getTypeOfDottedName`. The `TS2775` check in `resolveCallExpression` would apply the same rule, so an assertion through a name without an explicit type annotation in a comma expression gets the same error it already gets as a statement:
https://github.com/microsoft/TypeScript/blob/8d9b6da99ea7d4a8e7d906dd2532456dfe14e24f/tsc/internal/checker/checker.go#L8562

A call that is the value of a comma expression, as in `if (log(), isString(x))`, still goes through full checking. Type predicates there still narrow.

I have this change with a compiler test on a branch (https://github.com/u9g/TypeScript/tree/fix-comma-call-effects-recursion) and can open a PR if this goes to the Backlog. The investigation and patch were done with an AI coding assistant (Claude Code).

Escaped `in` / `instanceof` after a class field initializer is parsed as a binary operator instead of a new member

Keywords cannot contain escape characters, TS1260, escaped keyword, unicode escape in, instanceof, class field, ASI, automatic semicolon insertion

- This is the behavior in every version I tried (5.9.3, 6.0.2, 7.0.2 and 7.1.0-dev.20261020.3), and I reviewed the FAQ for entries about escaped keywords and ASI

https://www.typescriptlang.org/play/?ts=Nightly#code/MYGwhgzhAEDC0G8BQ1pmgXmgRhdAOgK4IBsAnAL4B2qtd0A9A2tAGYCWApiACbRVgAtpz4ADdlVF4ARpmgAmPEVKUqEAC5gqwTgHtWqJiw7c+A4WIkatO-VIpIkwXWt0hOAOhC6A5gAoAeWkAK05gdQ8Aa04ATwg-Kk4Adzg-AEoMgG5GZgBtACIwfIAaaHyJErLpSvK1TW09VnyAXSQgA

```
class C {
  a = 1
  \u{69}n          // a field named `in`
  b = 2
  \u{69}nstanceof  // a field named `instanceof`
}

console.log(Object.keys(new C())); // ["a", "in", "b", "instanceof"]
```

```
error TS1260: Keywords cannot contain escape characters.
error TS1005: ';' expected.
```

TypeScript treats `\u{69}n` as the `in` operator and parses `a = 1 in b = 2`. It does the same for `\u{69}nstanceof`. Then it reports the escape as an error.

No errors. The class has four fields: `a`, `in`, `b` and `instanceof`.

A keyword can't be written with a Unicode escape ([5.1.5 Grammar Notation](https://tc39.es/ecma262/#sec-grammar-notation): "A code point in a terminal symbol cannot be expressed by a \ UnicodeEscapeSequence"). So `\u{69}n` is the IdentifierName `in`, not the `in` operator. It isn't allowed to continue the initializer, and it comes after a line break, so ASI ends the field there. `\u{69}n` is then the name of the next field, since a ClassElementName can be any IdentifierName.

V8 (Node.js) runs the code above as JavaScript and prints `["a", "in", "b", "instanceof"]`.

- TypeScript already accepts the escaped form when it doesn't follow an initializer. `class C { \u{69}n = 1 }` and `class C { \u{69}n() {} }` have no errors. Only the continue-the-binary-expression path after a field initializer gets it wrong.
- Without the escape, `in` on the next line does continue the initializer (`a = x` / `in` / `z` is `a = x in z`). That part is correct and covered by test262's `fields-asi-5.js`.
- Related but different: #54196 (escaped `constructor` reported as TS1260).
- Babel had the same bug and fixed it in [babel/babel#18365](https://github.com/babel/babel/pull/18365). That PR found this TypeScript bug through typescript-eslint, which fails to parse Babel's new fixture with "Keywords cannot contain escape characters".

Drafted with the help of LLM and I have reviewed this issue and verified that the content is correct.

Content mappers: go-to-definition on an module specifier returns nothing when the target file has more than one span-map segment

> [!NOTE]
> Investigated with Claude (via Claude Code); corrections welcome.

`content mapper`, `go to definition`, `module specifier`, `IsSingleSegment`

- Works: `7.1.0-dev.20260821.1`
- Broken: `7.1.0-dev.20260822.1` through `7.1.0-dev.20261015.1` (bisected on nightlies)
- The only content-mapper change in that range is #63936 (Content mappers round 2).

Repro in [ember-content-mapper](https://github.com/NullVoxPopuli/ember-content-mapper) (draft PR NullVoxPopuli/ember-content-mapper#41, which is on `20261015.1`):

```
pnpm install
node --test test/lsp.js   # "go to definition from a .ts import into a .gts module"
```

The test sends `textDocument/definition` from `tsc --lsp --stdio` on the specifier in:

```
// examples/nvp-app/app/components/index.ts
export { default as Counter } from "./counter.gts";
//                                   ^ definition here
```

- `./counter.gts` (has a `<template>`, so the mapper returns many segments): `[]`
- A `./plain.gts` added next to it (`export const plain = 1;`, no template, so one verbatim segment): `plain.gts` at 0:0
- Go-to-definition on the `Counter` name in the same line works.

Go-to-definition on the specifier goes to the target file, as it does for `.ts` files and as it did on `20260821.1`.

#63936 removed the fallback that returned the top of the file for unmapped results. It said mappers should instead map "a zero-length range at the top of the file with `SpanMapFeature.Definition`". That doesn't help here, because a zero-length range is never requested:

1. For a module specifier, the declaration is the target `SourceFile`. In `createDefinitionLocations` (`tsc/internal/ls/definition.go`), `GetNameOfDeclaration` returns nil, so `name` is the `SourceFile` itself.
2. `createRangeFromNode(name, file)` gives `[first token, end of file]`. That is the whole virtual text after leading trivia.
3. `sourceFileRangeToLSPLocationForFeature` maps that range, and `if !selectionFidelity.IsSingleSegment() { continue }` drops it unless one segment covers the whole range.

A transformed file almost always has more than one segment, and segments can't overlap. So a mapper can't make this work: the target is dropped no matter what it emits. We tried mapping the virtual prefix to `[0, 0)` with `Definition`, with and without the feature flag, and with zero-length and non-zero virtual spans. All of them returned `[]`.

A possible fix: for a `SourceFile` declaration in a content-mapped file, use a zero-length range at original position 0. Do not map the whole file's range.

`--stableTypeOrdering`: `unknown || {}` is assignable to `Record<string, T>` in 6.0.3 with the option, and not in 7.0.2 nor in 6.0.3 without it

stableTypeOrdering, subtype reduction, empty object literal, `unknown || {}`, "Index signature for type 'string' is missing in type '{}'", 6.0 vs 7.0 difference

- `typescript@6.0.3` with `--stableTypeOrdering`: no error.
- `typescript@6.0.3` without it: TS2322.
- `typescript@7.0.2` (with or without the option) and `7.1.0-dev.20261011.1`: TS2322.

So the option makes 6.0 disagree with 7.0 on code where 6.0 without it agrees.

_No response_ (it takes two compiler versions)

```
// tsconfig: { "compilerOptions": { "strict": true, "noEmit": true } }, plus "stableTypeOrdering": true for the first case
declare const u: unknown;
const value = u || {};
const record: Record<string, number> = value;
```

The order of the operands does not matter, only the pair of types that is reduced:

```
declare const u: unknown;
declare const cond: boolean;
if (u) {
    const first = cond ? {} : u;
    const second = cond ? u : {};
    const r1: Record<string, number> = first;  // both lines: no error in 6.0.3 with the option,
    const r2: Record<string, number> = second; // TS2322 in 6.0.3 without it and in 7.0.2
}
```

```
$ tsc -p tsconfig.json                      # 6.0.3, "stableTypeOrdering": true
$ echo $?
0

$ tsc -p tsconfig.json                      # 6.0.3 without the option, and 7.0.2
repro.ts(3,7): error TS2322: Type '{}' is not assignable to type 'Record<string, number>'.
  Index signature for type 'string' is missing in type '{}'.
```

The type of `u || {}` prints as `{}` in the three cases, but it is not the same `{}`. The union that is reduced has two members that are subtypes of each other: the empty object type that a truthy `unknown` narrows to, and the type of the object literal. 6.0.3 without the option and 7.0.2 keep the first one, which has no implicit index signature. 6.0.3 with the option keeps the type of the literal, which has one, so the assignment is accepted.

`--stableTypeOrdering` exists so that 6.0 orders types as 7.0 does, so I expected 6.0.3 with the option to report what 7.0.2 reports (and here also what 6.0.3 reports without it).

What I checked in the sources, in case it helps:

- `compareTypes` and `compareSymbols` in `checker.ts` of v6.0.3 read the same as `CompareTypes` and `compareSymbolsWorker` of 7.0.2 for this pair: two object types, one without a symbol, which goes last. `removeSubtypes` is also the same loop in both. So the order of the two members should be the same, and yet the member that survives is not; I did not find where they diverge.
- It does not show in `.d.ts` output or in error messages, which print `{}` either way. It shows where assignability is asked: here, and in tools that call `isTypeAssignableTo`. I found it comparing typescript-eslint on TypeScript 6 (run with `stableTypeOrdering` to get the union order of 7.0 in messages) against the same rules on TypeScript 7: `no-unsafe-type-assertion` reports `(a.x || a.y || {}) as Record<string, T>` with 7.0.2 and with 6.0.3, and not with 6.0.3 plus the option.

Related: #64203 lists other defects of the option (closed as unactionable); none of them is this one.

Parser: exponential time and memory on nested `a < (b = …)` (failed type argument speculation is retried)

"parser exponential time", "parser out of memory", "type arguments speculation", "instantiation expression parse slow"

- This changed between versions 4.6.4 and 4.7.4 (likely #47607, "Instantiation expressions")

- Reproduces in 4.7.4, 5.9.3, 6.0.3, 7.0.2, and `7.1.0-dev.20261012.1` (`typescript@next`)

`ts.createSourceFile` time for the code below, with nesting depth n:

| n | 3.3.4000 | 4.6.4 | 4.7.4 | 5.9.3 | 6.0.3 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 10 | 6 ms | 10 ms | 86 ms | 72 ms | 72 ms |
| 12 | 6 ms | 9 ms | 667 ms | 511 ms | 516 ms |

The input is valid TypeScript with no errors; only the nesting depth matters. Here n = 14 (183 bytes):

```
declare let a: any, b: any, x: any;
x = a < (b = a < (b = a < (b = a < (b = a < (b = a < (b = a < (b = a < (b = a < (b = a < (b = a < (b = a < (b = a < (b = a < (b = 0))))))))))))));
```

Parse time and memory grow about 3× with each nesting level. Numbers for `tsc` 7.0.2 (native); the file reports no errors:

| n (bytes) | Parse time | Max RSS |
|---|---|---|
| 6 (103) | 0.01 s | 0.11 GB |
| 13 (173) | 0.90 s | 1.7 GB |
| 14 (183) | 2.8 s | 4.8 GB |
| 15 (193) | 8.0 s | 14.5 GB |

`typescript@next` behaves the same. Malformed input grows even faster, about 5× per level. `"a=b<c<(".repeat(11)` is 77 bytes and takes 13.8 s and 21.6 GB.

A single small file can therefore make the compiler or the language server hang, and then run out of memory.

To be clear, I don't think people write such code by hand. Depth up to about 6 costs nothing measurable. I found this by fuzzing a tool built on a TS parser, not from a real codebase. It can still come from generated code, from code mid-edit in an editor, or from untrusted input to services that parse TypeScript.

Parse time and memory stay roughly proportional to the input size.

`standalone/`:

In our ~12k-file Next.js app, this one call made `tsc --noEmit` take 153 s and 49.7 GB RSS on 7.0.2, against 58 s and 5.4 GB on 6.0.3. With `--checkers 1`, 7.0.2 created 46.6M types against 6.0.3's 1.77M. Typing the callback parameter (`(plugin: AnySlatePlugin) =>`) brings 7.0.2 back to 1.76M types.

Only the object-literal argument is affected. In the 14-plugin Plate case:

| argument | 6.0.3 types | 7.0.2 types |
|---|---:|---:|
| `configure({})`, `configure({ key: undefined })` | 31K | 667K |
| `configure(empty)`, where `const empty = {}` | 31K | 31.5K |
| `configure({} as {})` / `({} as any)` / `(null!)` / `(() => ({}))` | 29–31K | 29–31K |

7.0 should create about as many types as 6.0 here, or at least not grow faster with the number of union members. The input program is the same, and only the order of union constituents changed between versions.

What I think happens, from reading the 7.0 checker and a `--pprofDir` CPU profile:

1. `plugin.configure` on a union of N plugin types combines the N signatures, intersecting their parameter types: `(F1 | O1) & (F2 | O2) & …`, where `Fi` is the callback type and `Oi` is the config type. That normalizes to a union of 2^N intersections. 6.0 and 7.0 both do this, and both hit TS2590 when N is 18 or more distinct types.
2. For an object-literal argument, `checkObjectLiteral` calls `getApparentTypeOfContextualType` and then `discriminateContextualTypeByObjectMembers`, which calls `getPropertiesOfType(contextualType)`. `getPropertiesOfUnionOrIntersectionType` enumerates the properties of the **first** union constituent only. For each property name, `createUnionOrIntersectionProperty` calls `getTypeOfSymbol` on that property in every constituent. Each constituent is an intersection, so each call creates a new intersection type.
3. Which constituent comes first decides the cost:
   - **6.0** orders constituents by type id. Here the all-callback intersection `F1 & F2 & …` comes first. It has no properties, so step 2 does nothing.
   - **7.0** orders them structurally (`CompareTypes`): aliased or named types sort before anonymous ones, and intersections sort by their constituent lists. The all-config intersection `O1 & O2 & …` therefore comes first, and every property is resolved across all 2^N constituents.

In the 14-plugin Plate repro, the profile attributes 65% of check time to this path:

```
checkObjectLiteral → getApparentTypeOfContextualType → discriminateContextualTypeByObjectMembers → getPropertiesOfType → getPropertiesOfUnionOrIntersectionType → createUnionOrIntersectionProperty → getTypeOfSymbol → getIntersectionType → getCrossProductIntersections
```

The ordering, not a logic difference, explains the gap. If `src/plugin.d.ts` becomes a checked `src/plugin.ts`, 6.0 resolves `Config<K>` first while checking the alias declaration. Its first constituent is then the config intersection, and 6.0 creates as many types as 7.0: 205,225 vs 205,251 at 12 × 24. So 6.0 has the same exponential behavior and avoided it only because of the order it created types in.

Possible directions: skip or bound the optional-member discrimination in `discriminateContextualTypeByObjectMembers` when the contextual union is very large. Alternatively, avoid resolving union properties in a way that depends on which constituent sorts first.

Possibly related: #63749, another 7.0 issue that depends on type order.

Class names `eval` and `arguments` are not reported as invalid strict mode bindings

class name eval arguments, class arguments strict mode, TS1210 class name, TS1215 class declaration, checkStrictModeEvalOrArguments class

- This is the behavior in every version I tried (4.0.8, 5.0.4, 6.0.2, 7.1.0-dev.20261006.1), and I reviewed the FAQ for entries about strict mode and reserved words

https://www.typescriptlang.org/play/?ts=6.0.0-dev.20260416#

```
class arguments {}        // no error, expected TS1210
class eval {}             // no error, expected TS1210
const C = class eval {};  // no error, expected TS1210
declare class eval {} // no error, expected TS1210

// For comparison, all other strict-mode bindings are reported:
function f() {
  class D { m(arguments: number) {} } // TS1210
}
export {};
```

No errors are reported for the class names. The emitted JavaScript is rejected at runtime:

```
$ node out.js
SyntaxError: Unexpected eval or arguments in strict mode
```

The same happens in a `.js` file with `checkJs` enabled.

Each class name `eval` / `arguments` should be reported, as other strict mode bindings already are. Per the spec, all parts of a class are strict mode code ([ECMA-262 §11.2.2](https://tc39.es/ecma262/#sec-strict-mode-code)), and it is an early error for a `BindingIdentifier` in strict mode code to be `eval` or `arguments` ([§13.1.1](https://tc39.es/ecma262/#sec-identifiers-static-semantics-early-errors)). This applies to both class declarations and class expressions.

In the binder, function names (`checkStrictModeFunctionName`), variable declarations (`bindVariableDeclarationOrBindingElement`) and parameters (`bindParameter`) all call `checkStrictModeEvalOrArguments`. `bindClassLikeDeclaration` never does, so class names skip this check.

`bindWorker` already sets `inStrictMode = true` for `ClassDeclaration` / `ClassExpression` before it calls `bindClassLikeDeclaration`. So a fix could follow `checkStrictModeFunctionName`: call `checkStrictModeEvalOrArguments(node, node.name)` in `bindClassLikeDeclaration` when not in an ambient context.

createModuleResolver, resolveModuleName callback, nested request, inProgressSnapshot, SyncConn, wrong module

- This is the behavior in every version I tried: `7.1.0-dev.20261003.1` and `7.1.0-dev.20261004.1` (commit `50d70a3`, the newest `typescript@next`), the synchronous API (`typescript/unstable/sync`), linux-x64, Node 26.8.2. Module resolver callbacks arrived in #64299, so earlier versions do not have this API.

The API is not in the playground. The reproduction is one file.

`package.json`:

```
{ "private": true, "type": "module", "dependencies": { "typescript": "7.1.0-dev.20261004.1" } }
```

`repro.mjs` writes 300 files that each import three siblings, then loads them with a `resolveModuleName` callback that asks a default resolver for the answer with the in-progress snapshot, as the "module resolver callbacks can delegate to another resolver" API test does. The callback always returns the right file itself and only counts whether the nested answer was right.

```
import { mkdirSync, rmSync, writeFileSync } from "node:fs";
import { join } from "node:path";
import { API } from "typescript/unstable/sync";

const N = 300;
const nested = process.argv[2] !== "local";
const dir = join(process.cwd(), "proj");
rmSync(dir, { recursive: true, force: true });
mkdirSync(dir, { recursive: true });
for (let i = 0; i < N; i++) {
[... 35 more lines]
```

On `7.1.0-dev.20261004.1`:

```
$ node repro.mjs
nested answers: 16 right, 884 for another request; program errors: 893 (first: Module '"./m1.js"' has no exported member 'v1'.)
$ node repro.mjs
nested answers: 27 right, 873 for another request; program errors: 889 (first: Module '"./m1.js"' has no exported member 'v1'.)
$ node repro.mjs local
no nested request; program errors: 0
$ GOMAXPROCS=1 node repro.mjs
nested answers: 900 right, 0 for another request; program errors: 0
```

Two answers go astray, and only when the callback makes a nested request. The nested `resolveModuleName` returns the answer to a different import, and the callback's own return value reaches the wrong import too: every callback returns the correct file, yet almost every import in the program is bound to another module.

Each nested request gets its own answer and each callback answer reaches the import it was asked for, so the program has 0 errors with any number of threads.

**Impact:** a resolver callback that delegates to another resolver, the pattern the API's own test shows, binds most imports to the wrong module once the loader uses more than one thread. Every type and diagnostic the tool reads from that program is then wrong, and no error says so. In the reproduction, 873 of 900 nested answers went to another request.

The program loader resolves imports from several goroutines, and each one calls the callback through [`SyncConn.Call`](https://github.com/microsoft/TypeScript/blob/50d70a3f5f453a79a4323b263165da51f656a4e3/tsc/internal/ipc/conn_sync.go#L170-L221). `Call` matches a response by method name, so it relies on `c.mu` to keep its request and its response together. When the client's callback makes a nested request, `Call` [releases `c.mu`](https://github.com/microsoft/TypeScript/blob/50d70a3f5f453a79a4323b263165da51f656a4e3/tsc/internal/ipc/conn_sync.go#L202-L212) while it handles that request. Another goroutine's `Call` then writes its own callback request, which the synchronous client handles inside its pending nested call. When the first nested request finishes, its response reaches the client while the client waits for the second callback's nested answer, and the two callback responses then reach the wrong goroutines because they share a method name.

import defer, deferred import, side-effect import, import phase

- This is the behavior in every version I tried: 5.9.3 and 7.1.0-dev.20261004.1.

https://www.typescriptlang.org/play/?module=99&target=99#code/JYWwDg9gTgLgBAEwKYDMlTgIgHQHoCG2AVgM6YDcAUEA

```
import defer "./a.js";
```

No error. The output leaves out `defer`, so the module is evaluated eagerly:

```
import "./a.js";
```

An error. The [import defer proposal](https://github.com/tc39/proposal-defer-import-eval) only allows a namespace import after `defer` (`import defer * as ns from "./a.js"`), so this is a syntax error in JavaScript. Babel rejects it (`Unexpected token, expected "{"`).

TypeScript 7.1 already reports an error for the same form with the source phase:

```
import source "./b.wasm";
// error TS18111: A source phase import must specify a local binding.
```

In [`tryParseImportClause`](https://github.com/microsoft/TypeScript/blob/50d70a3f5f453a79a4323b263165da51f656a4e3/tsc/internal/parser/parser.go#L2403-L2416), a phase without bindings keeps an empty import clause only for `source`. For `defer`, the function returns `nil`, so the declaration has no import clause, and its phase is lost. [`checkGrammarImportClause`](https://github.com/microsoft/TypeScript/blob/50d70a3f5f453a79a4323b263165da51f656a4e3/tsc/internal/checker/grammarchecks.go#L2108-L2119) also has no check for a deferred import without bindings: it reports a default import (TS18058) and named imports (TS18059) only.

Keeping the empty import clause for `defer` too, and reporting an error for it in `checkGrammarImportClause`, would match `import source "./b.wasm"`.

Declaration emit re-walks a package.json `exports` map for every declaration (module specifier cache not shared across node builders)

> [!NOTE]
> **AI disclosure:** the investigation, the reproduction, the measurements and this text were produced by an AI coding agent (Claude Code, by Anthropic) working on my machine at my direction. I'm filing it myself and will follow up on it personally.

declaration emit slow, exports map, package.json exports performance, tryGetModuleNameFromExports, module specifier cache, specifierCache, getSpecifierForModuleSymbol, NodeBuilder per declaration, drizzle declaration emit

- This is the behavior in every version I tried, and I reviewed the FAQ for entries about performance

Tried 6.0.3, 7.0.2 and 7.1.0-dev.20261003.1 (and `main` at `50d70a3f5f`). All pay for the repeated walk. When a file has several exported declarations, 7.x is slower than 6.0.3 (table below), because 6.0.3 kept the module specifier cache on the checker's symbol links and 7.x keeps it on the node builder, which declaration emit creates once per declaration.

_No response_ (needs a `node_modules` package with a large `exports` map)

A generator for a fake package (`fake-orm`, with an `exports` map of N entries, whose classes are declared in internal files and re-exported through `fake-orm/pg-core`, the way ORM packages ship their types) and a project of `files` source files, each exporting `decls` inferred `table(...)` constants:

```
// node gen.mjs [exports=443] [files=700] [decls=1] [kinds=16] [cols=47]
// Writes node_modules/fake-orm (an `exports` map with `exports` entries) and src/*.ts.
import { mkdirSync, rmSync, writeFileSync } from "node:fs";
import { dirname } from "node:path";

const [EXPORTS = 443, FILES = 700, DECLS = 1, KINDS = 16, COLS = 47] = process.argv.slice(2).map(Number);
for (const d of ["node_modules/fake-orm", "src", "out"]) rmSync(d, { recursive: true, force: true });
const write = (p, text) => (mkdirSync(dirname(p), { recursive: true }), writeFileSync(p, text));
const pkg = "node_modules/fake-orm";

[... 50 more lines]
```

```
mkdir repro && cd repro && cp /path/to/gen.mjs .
node gen.mjs 443 700 1      # exports entries, files, declarations per file
npx -p typescript@next tsc -p .
```

Declaration emit time is dominated by `tryGetModuleNameFromExports`, which walks every entry of `fake-orm`'s `exports` map (and ends in "blocked by exports") once per emitted declaration × package-internal module that the declaration's type references. The answer is the same every time.

Wall-clock time for `tsc -p .`, default settings, macOS arm64 (M1 Max), single runs:

| Shape (`node gen.mjs …`) | 6.0.3 | 7.0.2 | 7.1.0-dev.20261003.1 |
|---|---|---|---|
| 443 entries, 700 files × 1 declaration | 29.2 s | 9.6 s | 7.0 s |
| 443 entries, 25 files × 8 declarations | 1.8 s | 2.3 s | 2.2 s |
| 1 entry, 700 files × 1 declaration (control) | 5.6 s | 0.7 s | 0.7 s |

Rows 1 and 3 emit identical declarations; only the size of the `exports` map differs. With `--checkers 1`, 7.0.2 reports `Emit time: 26.1s` for the first shape. A CPU profile of an earlier variant of this repro put 65% of CPU under `tryGetModuleNameFromExports` (about 1.3 ms per walk of a 450-entry map, ~11.9K walks). Cost scales linearly with the number of `exports` entries, the number of exported declarations, and the number of distinct package-internal modules per declaration, and does not depend on how many references are printed.

On a real project (declarations for a 716-table Drizzle schema; `drizzle-orm` has 443 `exports` entries) declaration emit takes 26–27 s of a 32 s build.

Mapping a file back through a package's `exports` map should happen about once per (package.json, target file, conditions), not once per emitted declaration and importing file, so the size of the map stops mattering.

Where the time goes (`main` at `50d70a3f5f`):

1. The module specifier cache (`NodeBuilderSymbolLinks.specifierCache`) lives on `NodeBuilderImpl` ([nodebuilderimpl.go#L107](https://github.com/microsoft/TypeScript/blob/50d70a3f5f453a79a4323b263165da51f656a4e3/tsc/internal/checker/nodebuilderimpl.go#L107), [#L1298](https://github.com/microsoft/TypeScript/blob/50d70a3f5f453a79a4323b263165da51f656a4e3/tsc/internal/checker/nodebuilderimpl.go#L1298)), but `EmitResolver` creates a new node builder for every declaration ([emitresolver.go#L958](https://github.com/microsoft/TypeScript/blob/50d70a3f5f453a79a4323b263165da51f656a4e3/tsc/internal/checker/emitresolver.go#L958), `// TODO: cache per-context`), so the cache never survives to the next declaration. 6.0.3 kept it in `getSymbolLinks(symbol).specifierCache` on the checker.
2. Even with that cache shared, its key includes the importing file, so one declaration per file still walks the map once per file × internal module. The walk itself ([specifiers.go#L903](https://github.com/microsoft/TypeScript/blob/50d70a3f5f453a79a4323b263165da51f656a4e3/tsc/internal/modulespecifiers/specifiers.go#L903) → [`tryGetModuleNameFromExports`](https://github.com/microsoft/TypeScript/blob/50d70a3f5f453a79a4323b263165da51f656a4e3/tsc/internal/modulespecifiers/specifiers.go#L1003)) does not depend on the importing file: only on the target file, the package, the conditions (from the options and import mode), the options and the host's case sensitivity.

I have a fix for both (two small commits: move the node builder's symbol links onto the `Checker`; memoize the exports lookup on the `packagejson.PackageJson`, keyed by every input of the walk). On the shapes above it gives 1.5 s / 0.2 s / 0.7 s (and `Emit time: 1.6s` with `--checkers 1`) with byte-identical declarations, and 26–27 s → 5 s emit on the real project. I'd like to open a PR if this is accepted.

Reverse-mapped inference exposes private members as public; since #63932 this rejects `f<T>() as C`

reverse mapped type private member, resolveReverseMappedTypeMembers, private is private in type but not in type, TS2352 private intersection readonly, inference private property public, keyof private member, syntheticProtectedProperties, 63932

- This changed in commit or PR 8239985a01 ("Fix `getDeclarationModifierFlagsFromSymbolEx` for synthetic properties", #63932), found by `git bisect` from 87e83b762 (good) to 1f70213d49 (bad), every step built and scored, none skipped.
- Still present on `main` at 09b1db061 (2026-10-01).
- TypeScript 6.0.3 (`tsc`) and `@typescript/native-preview` 7.0.0-dev.20260707.2 accept the code.

```
// @strict: true
class Entity {
    private secret = 1;
    markChanged(field: string): void {}
}
class Account extends Entity {
    emailAddress = '';
}
declare function getAccount<T extends object = object>(): Readonly<Account & T>;

[... 2 more lines]
```

On `main` (09b1db061) and since 8239985a01:

```
error TS2352: Conversion of type 'Readonly<Account & { secret: number; markChanged: (field: string) => void; emailAddress: string; }>' to type 'Account' may be a mistake because neither type sufficiently overlaps with the other.
  Property 'secret' is private in type 'Account' but not in type 'Readonly<Account & { secret: number; ... }>'.
```

The inferred `T` contains `secret` as a public property, which no `keyof`-based mapping could produce.

No error, as in TypeScript 6.0.3 and earlier native previews. `T` should be inferred without the private (or protected) members of `Account`, because a reverse mapping recovers the source of a mapped type keyed by `keyof`, and `keyof` never yields a private or protected member.

**Cause.** The assertion contextually types the call, so `T` is inferred by reverse-mapping `Account` through `Readonly<Account & T>`. `resolveReverseMappedTypeMembers` copies every source property, `secret` included. The copy has the member's declarations but no accessibility, so it reads as public.

That inferred `T` isn't new; what changed is what it does. Before #63932, the intersection property `secret` in `Account & T` resolved as private, `keyof` dropped it, and `Account` stayed comparable. After #63932, intersection properties take the most permissive accessibility (as `syntheticProtectedProperties.ts` asserts, deliberately), so the public copy wins and the comparison fails both ways. So #63932 isn't the bug; it exposed one.

Both conditions are required, which is why `Readonly<Class & object> as Class` alone doesn't reproduce it:

| variant | result |
|---|---|
| explicit `getAccount<object>()` (no inference) | no error |
| `Entity` without a private member | no error |
| inference + private member | TS2352 |

**Suggested fix.** Skip non-public source properties in `resolveReverseMappedTypeMembers`. That leaves #63932's accessibility rule untouched. I have a PR ready with a regression test and baselines, and the full pre-PR checklist passing.

**Real-world impact.** Hit in a real codebase on two casts of the shape `context.getAccount() as Account`, where an entity base class carries private members. The code is correct and type-checks under `tsc` 6.0.3.

TypeScript 7 VS Code extension: a workspace "typescript" 7.x package is not detected, only "@typescript/native-preview", which is no longer published

The TypeScript 7 extension finds a workspace's own TypeScript 7 only in `node_modules/@typescript/native-preview`. That package was last published on 2026-07-07 (`7.0.0-dev.20260707.2`). TypeScript 7 now ships as `typescript`: `typescript@7.0.2` came out the next day, and the 7.1 nightlies ship as `typescript@next` (`7.1.0-dev.20260930.4` today). So a project that installs TypeScript 7 the current way runs the extension's bundled compiler instead of its own. Nothing tells the user, and the only fix is to write a `tsdk` setting by hand.

**Versions:** TypeScript 7 extension 1.0.1, VS Code 1.140.0, macOS.

1. In an empty folder, run `npm install -D typescript@next` and add `main.ts` with `export const n: number = 1;`.
2. Open the folder in VS Code with the TypeScript 7 extension installed, and open `main.ts`. No setting is needed: on its first start, the extension turns TypeScript 7 on by itself (it writes `"js/ts.experimental.useTsgo": true` into the user settings). If TypeScript 7 was turned off later, run **TypeScript: Enable TypeScript 7 Language Server**.

**Expected:** the extension offers the workspace's TypeScript, as it does for `@typescript/native-preview`: the "This workspace has TypeScript 7 installed" prompt, and **Use Workspace Version** in **TypeScript: Select TypeScript Version**.

**Actual:** no prompt, and the server runs the extension's own compiler (7.0.2), not `node_modules/typescript` (7.1):

```
…/extensions/typescriptteam.native-preview-1.0.1-darwin-x64/lib/tsc --lsp --stdio
```

With `"js/ts.tsdk.path": "node_modules/typescript"`, the same project runs the workspace compiler. So only the detection is missing: `resolveTsdkPathToExe` already accepts a `typescript` package (bin `tsc`).

In `packages/vscode-typescript/src/session.ts` (main at 43521c80), `findWorkspaceNativePreviewPackages` checks only `node_modules/@typescript/native-preview`. Both `promptUseWorkspaceVersion` and the version picker (`promptSelectVersion`) use it.

Also detect `node_modules/typescript` when it is TypeScript 7 or newer. `pathHasTsserverJs` already tells a TypeScript 5 or 6 package apart from a TypeScript 7 one.

- The editor and the project's `tsc` (CLI, CI) then run the same compiler.
- Features that need a 7.1 nightly, such as content mappers with `--runExternalCode`, now need either the TypeScript 7 Nightly extension or a hand-written `tsdk` setting. The Nightly extension applies to every workspace and changes daily. The `tsdk` setting is easy to miss, because the extension never mentions it.

An optional `moduleSuffixes` array on a `contentMappers` entry:

```
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "moduleResolution": "bundler"
  },
  "contentMappers": [
    {
      "package": "identity-foo-mapper",
      "extensions": [".foo"],
      "moduleSuffixes": [".web", ""]
    }
[... 2 more lines]
```

For files with that entry's extensions, the entry's list is used instead of the `moduleSuffixes` compiler option, and each suffix goes in front of the extension, the way the compiler option already places it for `.ts`, `.tsx`, `.mts`, `.cts` and `.json`:

```
import { value } from "./card.foo"; // tries card.web.foo, then card.foo
```

What stays the same:

- Imports still name the mapped extension. Nothing is implied: `./card` stays unresolved.
- An entry without `moduleSuffixes` resolves exactly as today, including the compiler option's placement after the extension (#64548).
- The compiler option keeps applying to `.ts` and every other built-in extension, whatever the entry says.
- The mapper process takes no part in resolution. The list comes from the project's tsconfig, not from the mapper package.
- Today the key is ignored without an error, so no existing config depends on it.

Because the entry has its own list, the compiler option doesn't have to serve two purposes: a project can pick `.ios` variants of its `.ts` files and `.web` variants of its mapped files, or suffix only one of the two.

Platform variants in React Native-style projects: `Card.web.tsrx` and `Card.ios.tsrx` next to `Card.tsrx`, one per platform build. With the compiler option, TypeScript picks `target.web.ts` for `./target.ts`, but it cannot pick `card.web.foo` for `./card.foo`: the suffix is added after the whole file name (#64548). If a file with that name exists, the import resolves to it and fails:

```
// moduleSuffixes: [".web", ""], files card.foo and card.foo.web
main.ts(1,23): error TS6054: File '/repro/card.foo.web' has an unsupported extension. The only supported extensions are '.ts', '.tsx', '.d.ts', '.cts', '.d.cts', '.mts', '.d.mts', '.foo'.
main.ts(1,23): error TS7016: Could not find a declaration file for module './card.foo'. '/repro/card.foo.web' implicitly has an 'any' type.
```

So for mapped files the compiler option cannot select a variant today. The entry option gives them their own list without changing what the compiler option does.

The inferred declaration is:

During contextual typing, lookup of the `name` property through the reverse-mapped `Mapped<T>` constituent reaches the circular mapped-property guard, so `getTypeOfConcretePropertyOfContextualType` does not produce a contextual property type from that constituent.

The intersection-specific contextual typing logic introduced in #52095 can then consider applicable index information from other constituents. In this example, the index signature from `Indexed` provides `() => 0 | 1` as the contextual type of `name`.

That contextual type preserves the returned `0` as a literal type, which allows reverse inference to infer:

```
T = {
    name: 0;
}
```

and the call succeeds.

Before #52095, the same code reports TS2769 because no index-signature contextual type is supplied in this situation. As a result, `() => 0` is inferred as `() => number`, which is not assignable to `() => 0 | 1`.

There appear to be two potentially separate questions here:

1. Whether this reverse-mapped `name` property should reach the circular mapped-property guard at all.
2. If the circularity guard does apply, whether the resulting lack of a concrete contextual property type should allow the intersection logic to fall back to an index signature in the same way as when no concrete property exists.

I am not certain that the pre-#52095 TS2769 result is necessarily the desired behavior for this particular reproduction, since the currently inferred result is sound.

What seems unclear is whether the interaction between circular mapped-property handling and the index-info fallback introduced in #52095 is intentional.

In particular, these situations currently become indistinguishable to the subsequent intersection contextual-typing logic:

1. no concrete contextual property type is found because the property is absent
2. no concrete contextual property type is produced because property resolution was suppressed by the circular mapped-property guard

If those cases are intentionally meant to permit the same index-info fallback, then the current behavior is expected.

Otherwise, either:

- the reverse-mapped property may be reaching the circularity guard when it should not, or
- the reason that concrete property lookup produced no type may need to be preserved so that the intersection logic can distinguish circularity suppression from actual property absence.

The main question is therefore whether this interaction is intentional.

I found this while investigating my PR #64502, which deals with a different circular contextual-typing issue involving static properties.

While tracing contextual property lookup and circularity handling, I noticed that this reproduction reaches a path where lookup of the reverse-mapped property is suppressed by the circular mapped-property check, after which the intersection logic introduced by #52095 uses an applicable index signature as the contextual type.

I narrowed the observable behavior change down to #52095.

Language server retains the pre-edit program and its checkers for the rest of the session after the first edit

memory leak, language server, lsp, program clone, ReuseProgram, UpdateProgram, checker pool, retained program, projectReferenceFileMapper, RSS

- This is a memory retention bug in the native (Go) language server (`tsc --lsp`).
- Reproduces on `main` at 87f2e8ca9b.
- I haven't bisected it. It has been present since `projectReferenceFileMapper` started keeping a copy of the full `ProgramOptions`, and the language server started passing `CreateCheckerPool`/`CreateModuleResolver` closures that capture the project.

N/A (language server / memory behavior)

Any project with a `tsconfig.json` shows this. Minimal case:

```
// tsconfig.json
{}
```

```
// index.ts
console.log('Hello, world!');
```

Steps:
1. Start `tsc --lsp --stdio` and open `index.ts`.
2. Request diagnostics, hover or completion so the server creates checkers.
3. Edit `index.ts`, for example insert a newline, so the program is updated by cloning (`ProgramUpdateKindCloned`).
4. Wait past the checker idle timeout (30s) and force a GC.
5. The program from before the edit, its checker pool and its checkers are all still reachable.

After the first edit, the program from before the edit is never garbage collected. Neither are its checker pool or its checkers.

The reference chain is:

```
new Program
  → processedFiles.projectReferenceFileMapper   (shared with every clone by ReuseProgram)
  → opts.CreateCheckerPool                      (closure capturing the *project.Project)
  → old *Project → old Program → old checkerPool → old Checkers
```

`fileLoader.addProjectReferenceTasks` stores the whole `ProgramOptions` on the mapper (`opts: p.opts`). In the language server those options include the `CreateCheckerPool` and `CreateModuleResolver` closures, and both capture the project that created the program. `ReuseProgram` shares `processedFiles`, including the mapper, with every cloned program. So as long as a descendant clone is alive, the original program and everything it created stays reachable, typically until a full program rebuild.

The retained checkers are also never idle-cleaned. Their pool was already `Discard()`ed when the program was replaced, and that stops its idle-cleanup timer.

Measured on a ~500-file Next.js app. A scripted LSP client opened 5 files, requested diagnostics, hover and completion, and made one edit. Heap is `inuse_space` after GC; each figure is the average of 3 runs.

| | observed | with the retention removed |
|---|---|---|
| Go heap, active | ~541 MB | ~464 MB |
| Go heap, idle (after checker idle timeout) | ~471 MB | ~388 MB |
| RSS, idle | ~718 MB | ~600 MB |

I confirmed this with liveness tracking via `runtime.AddCleanup`. After the idle timeout, 2 programs, 2 checker pools and 2 checkers from the pre-edit program were still alive. The expected state is 1 program and 1 pool.

Once no snapshot references the pre-edit program, it should become unreachable and be garbage collected, together with its checker pool and checkers. Only the current program and its pool should stay alive. This is what `Snapshot.dispose` → `checkerPool.Discard()` is designed for: "allowing the pool and any idle checkers it still references to be reclaimed when the pool is garbage-collected".

The mapper only reads `opts.Config`, `opts.Host` and `opts.UseSourceOfProjectReference`. It never calls the factory closures, so clearing `CreateCheckerPool` and `CreateModuleResolver` from the copy of the options it keeps breaks the chain without changing behavior.

I have a fix with a regression test. The test edits a file so the program is cloned, then asserts the pre-edit program is garbage collected. It fails before the fix and passes after, and I'm happy to send it as a PR.

Possibly related: microsoft/typescript-go#3032 (LSP memory growth on large projects, root cause never identified).

# [API] `getJSDocCommentsAndTags` is no longer exposed

`ts.getJSDocCommentsAndTags(node)` finds the right JSDoc comment for a declaration (walking up through parents when the comment isn't syntactically on `node` itself ) and returns the comment node itself when appropriate, so callers can read its free-text description alongside its tags.

```
/**
 * The answer to everything.
 * @deprecated use theAnswer instead
 */
export const answer = 42;
```

The comment above attaches to the `VariableStatement`, not the `VariableDeclaration` for `answer`. Even so, `ts.getJSDocCommentsAndTags(declaration)` → one `JSDoc` node with both the description and the tag.

`getJSDocCommentsAndTags` does not exist / is not exported.

The closest alternative, `getJSDocTags(node)`, isn't enough: it walks up to the right ancestor internally, but only returns tags, never the `JSDoc` node — so the description is discarded even though it found the right comment.

Export a function equivalent to classic `getJSDocCommentsAndTags`, same ancestor-walking as `getJSDocTags`, but returning `(JSDoc | JSDocTag)[]` instead of always flattening to tags, so a description can be recovered without reimplementing the walk ourselves.

`getJSDocCommentsAndTags` was made public in classic `typescript` via #53627, fixing #45197 ("Add a way to get JSDoc comment text"), specifically so external tools (TypeDoc) could get a doc comment's description text instead of only its tags. The native `typescript` API doesn't have this function, and its one exported equivalent (`getJSDocTags`) reintroduces the same gap #45197 was filed for.

Type-check time for a chain of generic calls grows exponentially with the number of calls when the spec argument's inferred type carries a string index signature (`& { [key: string]: unknown }`). A 13-call chain checks in 0.12s; 20 calls take ~127s (~2.7x per added call). Removing the index signature from the spec type makes the same 20-call program check in ~15s.

and chains 20 `.command(...)` calls; each call after the third reads `ctx.s3?.text ?? ""`.

Timings (Apple M2 Pro, macOS, `--noEmit`):

| calls | time |
| ----: | ---: |
| 13 | 0.12s |
| 14 | 0.36s |
| 15 | 0.97s |
| 16 | 2.58s |
| 20 | 126.5s |

Ablation: deleting `& { [pluginField: string]: unknown }` from `CommandSpec` gives 20 calls in 14.9s (still superlinear, ~8.5x cheaper).

`--generateTrace` on the 20-call file: 236 `recursiveTypeRelatedTo_DepthLimit` events and 760 `structuredTypeRelatedTo` events; nearly all checker self-time lands on the single chained call expression.

A workflow DSL with this shape (accumulated tuple, mapped ctx values, index-signature spec for plugin extension fields) produces ~20-call chains: checking four such files costs ~324s for a package's declaration build and ~400-840s for a workspace-wide type-aware pass. `typescript@6.0.0-beta` (JS) takes 1785s on the same files, so 7.0.2 is much faster, but the growth is still exponential and forces us to drop work from the hot path.

Time roughly linear in the number of chained calls (or at least polynomial with a small exponent), as in Chains of 13 or fewer today.
